title: Battery Health Center Manual
text: Battery Health Center Manual Battery Health Center is a native GNOME app for the battery in your laptop. It shows how healthy the battery is, lets you protect it with a charge limit and a schedule, and shows which apps are draining it. This manual explains every feature of the app, page by page, with screenshots. Battery Health Center's Overview page, the page the app opens on How to read this manual # New here? Start with Getting started . Looking for one page of the app? Pick it in the left menu. Each page of this manual follows the app's own pages, with every control explained. Looking for a setting, a file or a command? See Reference . Something is not working? See Troubleshooting and FAQ . Press / anywhere in the manual to search it. The pages of this manual # Page What it covers Getting started Install the app, open it for the first time and find your way around. Overview Your battery, charger and recommendations at a glance. Health Capacity, wear, cycle count, the long-term trend and calibration. Charging Charge limits, profiles, one-time full charges and pausing charging. Charging schedule Full when you need it, protected the rest of the time. Power Power mode, automatic power mode and GNOME's power-saving settings. Usage Battery history, sleep drain and which apps use the most energy. Notifications and preferences Choose which notifications you get and when. Reports and your data HTML battery report, CSV export and where everything is stored. Reference Keyboard shortcuts, command line, files and a glossary. Troubleshooting and FAQ Answers to the most common questions and problems. Privacy and security What stays on your computer and what the root helper can do. Principles # Native and light. Rust with GTK 4 and libadwaita. It follows your GNOME theme, light and dark. Private by design. Everything runs on your computer. The app makes no network requests and sends no telemetry. The only things that leave your computer are the links you click yourself, such as this manual. Careful with root. Only a small helper runs as root. It accepts nothing but validated values and writes only the battery's charge-limit files and its own configuration. Accessible. Screen reader names and descriptions, and charts that never rely on color alone. In your language. The app follows your system language: English, Spanish, German, French and Simplified Chinese. This manual is in English. Getting help # In the app, press F1 or click the ? button at the top of the sidebar to open this manual. Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue .

title: Getting started
text: Getting started Battery Health Center is a native GNOME app for the battery in your laptop. It shows how healthy the battery is, lets you protect it with a charge limit and a schedule, and shows which apps are draining it. This page gets you from zero to a running app. What you need # A laptop with a battery that Linux can read. Battery information works with any standard Linux battery driver. Without a battery the app shows a "No Battery Found" message. GNOME with GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5 or newer. It is developed and tested on Ubuntu 24.04, Zorin OS 18 and Linux Mint 22, and on Fedora 43 and newer. Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and Mint 21 are too old. Charge-limit support (optional). Setting a charge limit needs firmware that the Linux kernel exposes as charge_control_end_threshold (or charge_stop_threshold ). This is common on ThinkPads and many ASUS, Dell, Huawei, LG, Samsung and System76 laptops. When your laptop does not have it, the Charging page says "Not supported on this laptop" and everything else keeps working. Install # Ubuntu, Debian and derivatives (apt) # For Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian 13+, Linux Mint 22, Zorin OS 18 and other derivatives on 64-bit Intel/AMD: sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://arios4k.github.io/apt/key.asc | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/battery-health-center.asc > /dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/battery-health-center.asc] https://arios4k.github.io/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/battery-health-center.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install battery-health-center Updates arrive with sudo apt upgrade . The signing key fingerprint is F090 D01D 74F7 14C8 5A95 23CA 4773 367E BD97 6CF5 . Fedora (COPR) # sudo dnf copr enable arios/battery-health-center sudo dnf install battery-health-center Updates arrive with sudo dnf upgrade . The charge-limit and schedule services are turned on by the installation, so nothing else needs setting up. From source # See Build from source in the README. Note. If you installed an older version as a snap, remove it first with sudo snap remove battery-health-center . That deletes its history, so copy ~/snap/battery-health-center/current/.local/share/battery-health-center/*.csv to ~/.local/share/battery-health-center/ before you do. Your first launch # Open Battery Health Center from your applications. The first time, the app asks whether it should record history in the background . Choose Turn On if you want battery history, sleep drain and notifications to keep working with the window closed. The app then starts hidden when you log in. Choose Not Now to skip it. History is then only recorded while the window is open. You can change your mind any time with the Record History in the Background switch on the Usage page. Some pages need time to fill with data. Nothing is wrong when a chart is empty at first: What How long until it appears Battery level and power charts A sample is saved once a minute while the app runs. The chart starts the moment you open the app. Apps using significant energy A few seconds after you open the app. Capacity trend and the date the battery reaches 80% At least 5 daily readings spread over 14 days. The capacity is logged once a day, so open the app on different days or turn on background recording. Optimized charging At least 3 unplugs after a long charge on weekdays (and again on weekends) in the last 28 days. Sleep drain After the laptop sleeps on battery for at least 15 minutes while the app was running before and after. Finding your way around # The main window. The sidebar on the left switches between the five pages; the question-mark button opens this manual and the menu button opens the main menu. The sidebar has the five pages: Overview , Health , Charging , Power and Usage . Hover a page to read a one-line description of it. The help button (a question mark, at the top of the sidebar) opens this manual in your browser, at the page that matches the page you are on: on Charging it opens the Charging page. You can also press F1 or choose User Manual from the main menu. The main menu (three lines) has Refresh , Export Battery Report… , Export Data as CSV… , Preferences , User Manual , About Battery Health Center and Quit . Adaptive layout. Overview, Health and Usage use two columns in a large window. Charging and Power use one centered column so the settings stay in reading order. Below 820 logical pixels of width the columns stack, and below 600 pixels the sidebar becomes a back-navigation list, so the app also works in a narrow window. Light and dark. The app follows your GNOME appearance and accent color. In high-contrast mode it keeps the system palette. Save problems. If a preference or the history cannot be saved (for example, the disk is full), a banner at the top says so. Choose Details to see which file and why. The app retries history writes when storage recovers. The About dialog: copy the version number for a bug report, open the project page, report an issue, or read the license. Accessibility # The charge ring and the charts are exposed to screen readers as images with a name and a description (the latest value and what the colors mean). Level bars announce their value, icon-only buttons have names, and decorative icons are hidden. Chart colors keep at least 3:1 contrast on light and dark cards, periods on the charger are marked by a strip along the bottom of the chart so color is never the only signal, and the dark theme's accent keeps 4.5:1 with white button text.

title: Overview
text: Overview Overview is the page the app opens on. It answers "how is my battery doing right now?" without making you hunt for it. The Overview page. The left column is about right now; the right column is about the battery's long-term health and what you could do better. The charge ring # The ring shows the charge level. The headline and the line under it say what the battery is doing. The percentage is in the middle. The headline underneath is one of: Headline Meaning Charging The charger is connected and the battery is filling up. Below it you see the time left until full (or until your limit), for example "1 h 10 min until 80%", or the charging power in watts. On Battery The laptop is running from the battery. The line below estimates the time remaining at the current usage; while it is still measuring it says "Estimating time remaining…". Plugged In, Not Charging / Charging On Hold The charger is connected but charging is held on purpose, usually because the charge limit has been reached. The line below says "Charge limit of 80% protects your battery". Fully Charged The battery is at 100% and the charger is connected. Charging to 100% A one-time or scheduled full charge is running. Your limit comes back automatically. The time estimates are based on how fast the battery has been charging or draining recently, so they settle after a minute or two. Power source # The Power Source card names the charger and its rating. When a charger is connected, this card names it ( AC adapter or USB-C Power Delivery ) and shows its rating in watts, with volts and amps when the laptop reports them. Chargers that do not report a rating say "This charger doesn't report its power rating". The card also appears on battery and shows Last Seen Plugged In . Three more groups can show up on this page depending on the situation: Since Last Charge (on battery): how long ago you unplugged, how much of the battery you used, and the average draw in watts. Other Devices : the battery level of connected wireless devices such as a mouse or a keyboard, when Linux reports it. Two batteries : laptops with two batteries are supported. Battery health summary # A short health summary. The full picture is on the Health page. Maximum capacity compared with when the battery was new, its condition, and its cycle count. Open the Health page for explanations, the trend and calibration. Recommendations # Each recommendation says what it noticed and, where it can, has a button that fixes it. Recommendations are small, practical suggestions based on the current state. They only appear while they are true, and when there is nothing to suggest the card says Everything looks good . Recommendation When it appears Button Battery capacity is down to N% Maximum capacity is below 80%. Calibrating can correct a wrong reading; if it stays low, consider a replacement. Calibrate opens the calibration on the Health page. Limit charging to 80% The laptop is plugged in and no charge limit is set, and your battery supports one. Set Up opens the Charging page. Draining while plugged in The charger cannot keep up with the laptop's power use. Use a more powerful charger. None Low-power charger The charger is under 45 W, so charging can be slow, especially while you work. None High drain during sleep The laptop used a lot of battery while asleep (more than 2% per hour). Details opens the sleep list on the Usage page. An app is using significant energy An app is keeping the CPU busy on battery. Quitting apps you are not using makes the battery last longer. Details opens the app on the Usage page. Performance mode is on You are on battery in Performance mode, which drains faster. Balanced is usually enough. Use Balanced Screen brightness is at N% On battery with the brightness at 80% or more. The screen is usually the biggest power user. Lower to 50% Keyboard backlight is on On battery with the keyboard backlight on. Turn Off Bluetooth is on but nothing is connected On battery with Bluetooth enabled and no device connected. Turn Off Battery is low The battery is low and not charging. Regularly running it flat wears it faster. None Tip. The brightness, keyboard backlight and Bluetooth suggestions only appear on battery, and only when your desktop exposes those controls.

title: Health
text: Health Every battery loses a little capacity with age. The Health page measures how much, shows how it has changed over time, and tells you when it is worth doing something about it. The Health page: capacity and usage on the left, the long-term trend and battery details on the right. Capacity # The Capacity card compares what the battery holds now with what it held when new. Maximum Capacity is the energy the battery holds when full now, as a percentage of what it held when it was new, shown with a level bar. Full Charge Capacity is that energy in watt-hours (Wh). Design Capacity is what the manufacturer rated the battery for when new. Capacity Lost is the difference in Wh and in percent. Condition turns the number into a plain word: Condition Maximum capacity What it means Normal 80% or more The battery is functioning normally. Worn 60% to 80% The battery holds less charge than when new but works normally. Service Recommended Under 60% The battery holds significantly less charge; consider replacing it. Note. Some drivers report charge in µAh (charge-based) and others in µWh (energy-based). The app supports both. Capacity over time and the trend # Capacity is recorded once a day. The dashed line marks 80%, the usual point where a battery is considered worn. The app records the maximum capacity once a day (the first time it runs that day) and plots it. Readings wobble a little from day to day, so the line is the direction that matters, not any single point. After at least 5 daily readings spanning at least 14 days the Trend row switches from progress ("3/5 readings · 6/14 days") to a result: N% per month , the rate at which capacity is falling, and Reaches 80% : the month and year the battery is projected to cross 80% ("Around March 2028"). Not declining when the line is flat or rising. Already below 80% when it has already crossed. A battery that does not report capacity data shows "This battery does not report capacity data, so a health trend cannot be calculated." Tip. Turn on Record History in the Background on the Usage page so the daily reading is saved even on days you never open the window. Usage # Cycle count and live electrical readings. Cycle Count is how many full charge-and-discharge equivalents the battery has been through. Most laptop batteries are rated for 300–1000 cycles. Current Charge is the energy in the battery now, in Wh. Average Draw on Battery (24 h) is the average power the laptop used while on battery over the last day. It appears once there is enough history. Voltage and Minimum Design Voltage : the present voltage and the lowest voltage the battery is designed to reach. Rows the battery does not report are shown as "Not reported", and rows with no history yet say "No data yet". Battery information # The details of the battery itself. The serial number is hidden in this screenshot. Manufacturer, model, serial number, chemistry (for example Li-ion or Li-poly) and the device name Linux uses ( BAT0 ). It is handy for warranty claims and when you shop for a replacement. Calibration # Start a guided calibration from the Calibration card. Battery gauges estimate the charge. When the percentage jumps around, or the laptop shuts down before it reaches 0%, the estimate has drifted. Calibration lets the battery relearn its true capacity. It takes a full charge, a full discharge and another full charge, usually a few hours in total, and you can use the laptop normally in between. Choose Start and confirm Start Calibration? . If the laptop is not full, plug it in; the card shows "Step 1 of 3: Charge to 100%". When the battery is full you get the notification Calibration: Unplug Your Laptop . Unplug the charger and use the laptop until the battery is nearly empty (5%). The card shows "Step 2 of 3" with the current percentage. At 5% you get Calibration: Plug In Now . Connect the charger and let it charge to 100% again. You get Calibration Complete . The battery's capacity reading has been recalibrated, and your charge limit is back on. The confirmation explains the three steps before anything starts. Careful. During calibration the charge limit is lifted so the battery can reach 100%. Choose Cancel on the card at any time to stop; your limit returns. Hardware. Calibration needs a battery that reports its charge accurately. It is a fix for a wrong reading, not for a battery that has genuinely worn out: if the maximum capacity stays low afterwards, that number is the truth.

heads.t: Capacity over time and the trend

title: Charging
text: Charging Lithium batteries wear faster when they sit at full charge. If your laptop is plugged in most of the day, limiting the charge to about 80% can noticeably extend the battery's lifespan. This page sets that limit. The Charging page is one centered column: status first, then the limit, the schedule and the behavior controls. Hardware. Charge limits need firmware support that Linux exposes as charge_control_end_threshold . If your laptop does not have it, this page shows Not supported on this laptop with the reason, and the rest of the app works normally. Charging status # The three cards at the top tell you what is in force right now. Active Charge Limit : where charging stops for each battery. "Charging will stop at 80%", or "Charge limit removed" when there is no limit. Next Scheduled Full Charge : when your schedule will next lift the limit, as "Full by Mon 07:30 · starts Mon 05:30". It says "Save a charge limit below 100% to use scheduled charging" when a schedule would have no limit to lift, and "Learning your routine" while optimized charging is still gathering data. Temporary Override : "None" normally. During a one-time full charge it says "One-time full charge", with the limit that comes back; during a scheduled full charge it says "Scheduled full charge". Charge limit # Pick a profile, or switch on Limit Maximum Charge and set your own numbers, then choose Apply. Profiles # The Profile menu sets both numbers at once: Profile Stops charging at Resumes below Best for Maximum Lifespan (60%) 60% 55% Plugged in most of the time. The least wear. Balanced (80%) 80% 75% A good everyday balance. Full Capacity (100%) 100% No limit The longest time away from the charger. Custom Your number Your number Your own settings below. Your own numbers # Limit Maximum Charge turns the limit on or off. When it is off, the battery charges to 100%. Stop Charging At (a percentage) is the level where charging stops. Resume Charging Below is the level where charging starts again. Keeping a gap avoids topping up after every small drop. It has to be below the stop level. Keep After Restart re-applies the limit when the computer starts and after it wakes from sleep. Without it the firmware may forget the limit when it restarts. A saved limit is also required for the schedule. Applying the limit # Pick a profile, or change the numbers. Choose Apply . Enter your password in the system prompt. Changing a charge limit writes to the battery's firmware settings, so it needs administrator permission. The prompt is the standard PolicyKit one. A message confirms "Charging will stop at 80%" (or "Charge limit removed"). Tip. Not every laptop has a separate resume level. When yours does not, Resume Charging Below is not shown. The page only offers the controls your laptop supports. Charge to 100% now # Need a full battery for a trip or a long day away from the charger? While a limit below 100% is in force, a Charge to 100% Now row appears with a Charge Now button. Connect the charger and choose Charge Now . The Overview says "Charging to 100%" and the Temporary Override card says "One-time full charge". When the battery is full, or when you unplug, your limit comes back by itself. Choose Back to your charge limit if you change your mind earlier. Charging behavior # Temporarily pause charging or run from the battery while plugged in. The While Plugged In menu is a temporary override for special situations: Choice What it does Normal Charges as usual, following your limit. Pause Charging The laptop stays plugged in and runs from the charger without charging the battery. Run on Battery The laptop runs from the battery even though the charger is connected. Useful for testing how long the battery lasts. Choose Normal to go back. This control only appears when your laptop supports it.

title: Charging schedule
text: Charging schedule A charge limit is great until the morning you need the laptop to last all day. The charging schedule gets you both: the limit protects the battery, and shortly before you need the laptop the limit is lifted so the battery is full on time, then put back. The Charging Schedule card: optimized charging, the ready-by times, and the lead time. Careful. The schedule needs a saved charge limit below 100%. Turn on Limit Maximum Charge and Keep After Restart on the Charging page, then choose Apply . Until then the schedule card tells you so. Ready-by times # A ready-by time is a day or group of days with the time you want the battery to be full by, for example Weekdays, 07:30 . Choose Add a Time… . Pick the days ( Mon to Sun ) and the time. At least one day must be selected. Choose Add . The time appears as a row such as "Full by 07:30 · Weekdays". Use the trash button on a row to remove it. Choose Save Schedule and enter your password once. Pick days and the time you want the battery to be full by. Days that share a time are shown together: Every day , Weekdays , Weekends , or a list of days. You can have up to 14 rules. Rules are saved only when you choose Save Schedule , and "Schedule saved" or "Schedule removed" confirms it. Start charging before # Start Charging Before is the lead time, in hours before each ready-by time, when the limit is lifted. The default is 2 hours; you can choose from half an hour to six hours. Pick a longer lead if your charger is slow or your battery is large. The limit stays lifted until the battery is full, you unplug, or 30 minutes after the ready-by time, whichever comes first, so a battery that is a bit slow still finishes. Then your limit is restored. The Charging Status card Next Scheduled Full Charge shows what will happen next, such as "Full by Mon 07:30 · starts Mon 05:30". Optimized charging # Do not want to enter times? Turn on Optimized Charging and the app learns your routine. Whenever you unplug after the laptop was plugged in for at least 3 hours , the app records the time. When it has seen at least 3 such unplugs in the last 28 days on weekdays (or on weekends) that are within an hour and a half of each other, it uses the earlier end of that range as the ready-by time for those days. The Learned So Far row shows the result: "Weekdays: charged by about 08:15", or "Weekends: still learning (2 of 3 unplugs)". Weekday and weekend habits are learned separately, so a lie-in on Saturday does not disturb your Monday. Everything stays on your computer, in a small file of unplug times. How it works # When you choose Save Schedule , the app asks for your password once and installs the schedule where a small systemd service can read it. That service runs as root only while a schedule exists (a systemd .path unit starts it), lifts and restores the limit at the right moments, and goes back to sleep. It needs no password each time and does not need the app to be running. The details are on Privacy and security .

title: Power
text: Power The Power page puts the most useful power options in one place: the power mode, a way to switch it automatically, and the GNOME settings that save the most battery. Everything here is shown only if your system supports it. The Power page is one centered column, like Charging. Power mode # Choose how the laptop trades performance for battery life. Power Saver, Balanced or Performance, using the same system service as GNOME's quick settings. Power Saver reduces performance to extend battery life. Performance is only offered on some laptops and drains the battery faster. The setting is shared with the GNOME panel, so a change made there shows up here and the other way around. Note. If the Power Profiles Daemon is not running, the page says "Power Mode and Automatic Power Mode Aren't Available", because the mode can neither be read nor changed. Automatic power mode # Switch the mode by itself when you plug in or unplug. Turn on Switch Automatically and the app changes the power mode when you plug in or unplug the charger. When Plugged In and On Battery : choose the mode for each state. A typical setup is Performance on the charger and Power Saver on battery. Use Power Saver When Battery Is Low overrides the on-battery mode once the charge falls to the Low Battery Level (20% by default). You can still change the mode by hand at any time. It is only switched again the next time something changes (the charger is connected or removed). Power saving # GNOME's own battery-saving settings. These are the same settings as Settings → Power , collected in one place: Setting What it does Power Saver When Battery Is Low GNOME switches to Power Saver mode when the battery gets low. Dim Screen When Inactive Dims the screen when you stop using the laptop. The screen is usually the biggest power user, so this saves a lot. Automatic Screen Brightness Adjusts the brightness to the light around you (needs an ambient light sensor). Screen Blank Turns the screen off after you stop using the laptop. Choose from 1 to 15 minutes, or Never. Automatic Suspend on Battery Sleeps after a time of inactivity on battery (5 minutes to 2 hours, or Never). Sleeping uses far less power than staying on. Automatic Suspend When Plugged In The same, on the charger. Power button and lid # What the power button and the lid do. Choose what happens when you press the power button and when you close the lid, separately on battery and on the charger. The options include Suspend , Hibernate , Turn Off the Screen , Shut Down , Log Out , Ask What to Do and Do Nothing ; you only see the ones your system supports. Top bar # Show the percentage next to the battery icon. Show Battery Percentage shows the percentage next to the battery icon in the GNOME top bar. Note. If GNOME's power settings cannot be found, this part of the page says "Power Saving and Power Button Settings Aren't Available". They need GNOME Settings Daemon. The page is the part of the app that is most tied to GNOME.

title: Usage
text: Usage The Usage page answers "where did my battery go?" It has the history of the battery level and power draw, how much the laptop used while asleep, and the apps that use the most energy. The Usage page: history on the left, apps on the right. Battery level and power # The history chart. Choose what to plot and how far back to look. Use the two button groups above the chart: Level plots the battery percentage. Power plots the power draw in watts: blue is power used on battery, green is charging power. 24 Hours or 7 Days sets the range. History is kept for 30 days. In the level chart, green is plugged in , blue is on battery , and a dashed line marks your charge limit. Periods on the charger also get a thick strip along the bottom, so the chart does not depend on color alone. Gaps are times when the app was not running. A new install says "Your history starts here" and "Not enough samples in this view yet" until the app has recorded a few minutes. A sample is saved every minute while the app runs. Record history in the background # One switch keeps history, sleep drain and notifications running with the window closed. History, sleep drain and notifications only work while Battery Health Center is running. This switch adds a login item that starts the app hidden when you log in, so everything keeps working with no window. Open the app from your applications at any time to bring the window up; the hidden copy hands over to it. After an update the hidden copy notices that its program file was replaced and restarts itself in the new version, within about a minute, once no window is open. Battery use during sleep # How much charge your laptop used while suspended. When the app is running before and after the laptop sleeps on battery for at least 15 minutes, it records the session: when it started, how long it slept, and how much battery it used, in percent and in percent per hour. The five most recent sessions are listed. High means more than 2% per hour. That is worth investigating, and you also get a notification and an Overview recommendation. Moderate is 1% to 2% per hour, and Normal is under 1% per hour. The Sleep Mode row says how your laptop sleeps: Mode Meaning Modern Standby (s2idle) Wakes quickly, but some laptops drain more while asleep. If your laptop also supports deep sleep, the row says so and mentions the kernel option mem_sleep_default=deep . Deep Sleep (S3) The lowest-power sleep mode. Shallow Sleep (S1) A light sleep mode. Tip. A laptop that loses a lot of charge asleep is a common complaint. Modern Standby is usually the cause; deep sleep, when available, typically uses much less battery. Apps using the most energy # Apps ranked by their current energy impact. The Using Significant Energy list at the top right is what to look at when the battery is draining fast right now. It ranks the apps by their current energy impact; when none stands out, it says "No apps are using significant energy". Click an app to see its detail. Energy Use by App: pick the period with the buttons. The Energy Use by App list covers a longer period: Since Opened (since the app started), 24 Hours or 7 Days . It shows the eight biggest. Each row has: the app's name and icon, and how many processes it has (a browser may have dozens); its CPU use in percent of one core, and the estimated energy used on battery; an impact label: High (40% or more), Medium (10% or more) or Low . System marks background services such as the Linux kernel. Careful. Linux does not measure power per app. Energy impact is estimated from CPU time, and watts are the measured battery drain above idle, shared between apps by CPU use. GPU, display and device activity are not measured per app. Treat the numbers as a guide, not as a measurement. The (i) button next to each list explains this in the app. Apps are grouped using the systemd scope that GNOME starts each app in. Apps that move their processes elsewhere (such as Chromium-based browsers) are grouped by their parent process, so a browser is one row, not fifty. App detail # Click an app to see its energy impact and estimated use hour by hour. Click any app to open its detail. It shows the Energy Impact and the Energy Used (an estimate in Wh on battery), with the period set by the 24 Hours / 7 Days buttons, and an hour-by-hour chart of CPU use and energy. Only hours when the app was running are shown, and completed hours are saved for the last 7 days. A new install says "No hourly history yet. Keep the app running to collect activity."

title: Notifications and preferences
text: Notifications and preferences Open Preferences from the main menu or with Ctrl + , to choose which notifications you get. Everything else in the app is on its own page. The Preferences dialog. Notifications # Notifications are sent while Battery Health Center is running. Turn on Record History in the Background on the Usage page to get them even when the window is closed. All of them are on by default; turn off any you do not want. Notification When you get it Charge Limit Reached Charging stops at your limit: "Charged to 80%. Charging has stopped at your limit to protect the battery." Fully Charged Without a Limit The battery is full and no limit is set: a reminder to unplug, or to set a charge limit to slow wear. Low Battery The battery drops to the Notify At level (20% by default) and you are not charging. It adds the time remaining when it knows it. Apps Using Significant Energy An app keeps the CPU very busy for a couple of minutes while you are on battery. Quit it if you are not using it. High Drain During Sleep The laptop used a lot of battery while asleep (over 2% per hour): "Your laptop used 7% in 51 min asleep (8.3% per hour)." Clicking a notification opens, or raises, the app window. Note. The calibration step notifications ( Unplug Your Laptop , Plug In Now , Calibration Complete ) are always sent, because you need them to complete the calibration. Other settings, found elsewhere # Setting Where Record history in the background Usage page Charge limit, schedule and charging behavior Charging page Power mode, automatic power mode, power saving Power page Where the settings are saved ~/.config/battery-health-center/settings.ini

title: Reports and your data
text: Reports and your data Your battery data belongs to you. Battery Health Center can export it as a readable report or as spreadsheet-friendly files, and it stores everything in plain files in your home folder. Battery report (HTML) # Choose Export Battery Report… from the main menu, pick a file name, and the app saves a single self-contained HTML page you can open in any browser, print, email or keep. It is useful for a warranty claim, or to show a buyer when you sell the laptop. A Open button in the confirmation opens it straight away. The report has these sections: Battery : a table for each battery with the manufacturer, model, chemistry, design and full-charge capacity, maximum capacity, condition, cycle count and more. Capacity Over Time : the daily capacity chart. Battery Level, Last 7 Days : the level chart with charger periods. Battery Use During Sleep : the recorded sleep sessions. Apps by Energy Use, Last 7 Days : the top apps with estimated use. The report is in English whatever your system language. Export data as CSV # Choose Export Data as CSV… , pick a folder, and choose Save Here . The app writes four files you can open in a spreadsheet or load into your own tools (the confirmation says how many files were saved): File Contents battery-history.csv Battery level and power samples, one per minute (kept for 30 days). capacity-history.csv The daily capacity readings used for the trend. sleep-sessions.csv Each recorded sleep session and how much battery it used. app-energy.csv Each app's CPU use and estimated energy, per hour (kept for 7 days). Timestamps use the ISO 8601 format with your time zone, for example 2026-11-07T08:15:00-05:00 . From the command line # Both exports also work without opening the window, which is handy for scripts and scheduled backups: battery-health-center --export-report report.html battery-health-center --export-csv ~/battery-data The CSV command prints the path of each file it wrote. Where your data is stored # Location What it holds ~/.local/share/battery-health-center/history.csv Battery samples, once a minute, for the last 30 days. ~/.local/share/battery-health-center/health.csv The daily capacity readings used for the trend. ~/.local/share/battery-health-center/app-history.csv Per-app energy by the hour, for the last 7 days. ~/.config/battery-health-center/settings.ini Your preferences. ~/.config/autostart/io.github.BatteryHealthCenter.desktop Present only when background recording is on. The charge limit and the schedule are stored by the root helper, outside your home folder (see Reference ). To start over, quit the app and delete the files you want to reset. Writes are made safely: preferences are replaced atomically, and if a save fails the app keeps the previous file, shows a banner with the path and the error, and retries the history when storage recovers.

title: Reference
text: Reference Keyboard shortcuts # Shortcut Action F1 Open this manual at the page for the one you are on Ctrl + R Refresh the readings now Ctrl + , Open Preferences Ctrl + Q Quit Tab , Shift + Tab , Enter Move between controls and activate them; the sidebar rows are keyboard-accessible too The main menu # Item What it does Refresh Reads the battery and everything else again right now. Export Battery Report… Saves the HTML report . Export Data as CSV… Saves the CSV files . Preferences Opens the notification settings . User Manual Opens this manual at the page for the one you are on. About Battery Health Center Version, links, credits and license. Quit Closes the app. Command line # Command What it does battery-health-center Open the window. battery-health-center --background Start hidden and keep recording history (this is what the login item runs). battery-health-center --export-report FILE.html Write the battery report and exit. battery-health-center --export-csv FOLDER Write the four CSV files into the folder and exit. Files and services # Path or unit Purpose /usr/bin/battery-health-center The app. bhc-helper The only part that runs as root. It validates its arguments and writes the charge-limit files and its own configuration. Started through PolicyKit. /etc/battery-health-center.conf The saved charge limit that Keep After Restart re-applies. /etc/battery-health-center.schedule The saved ready-by times and lead time. /var/lib/battery-health-center/unplug-log The unplug times learned by optimized charging. battery-health-center-restore.service Re-applies your limit at startup and after sleep. battery-health-center-scheduler.service and .path Run the schedule; the .path unit starts the service only while a schedule exists. /sys/class/power_supply/BAT* Where the battery readings come from (read directly; no root needed). The exact configuration file locations can differ slightly between packages; the How it works notes describe what each piece does. Glossary # Capacity (maximum capacity) How much energy the battery holds when full now, compared with when it was new. Design capacity What the manufacturer rated the battery for when new, in Wh. Cycle count The number of full charge-and-discharge equivalents. Two half charges make one cycle. Wh (watt-hour) A unit of stored energy. A 50 Wh battery can power a 10 W laptop for about five hours. Charge threshold A firmware setting for where charging stops (end threshold) and resumes (start threshold). Power profile The system's performance setting: Power Saver, Balanced or Performance. Energy impact An estimate of how much battery an app uses, based on its CPU time. Sleep drain Battery used while the laptop is suspended, as percent and percent per hour. s2idle, S3 and S1 Sleep states. s2idle (Modern Standby) wakes quickly, S3 (deep) uses the least power, S1 is a light sleep. Calibration A full charge, a full discharge and a full charge that lets the battery gauge relearn the real capacity. PolicyKit The standard Linux service that asks for your password before an app makes an administrator-level change.

title: Troubleshooting and FAQ
text: Troubleshooting and FAQ Frequently asked questions # Will the charge limit work on my laptop? # Battery information works on any laptop with a standard Linux battery driver. Charge limits need firmware support that the kernel exposes as charge_control_end_threshold (or charge_stop_threshold ), as on ThinkPads and many ASUS, Dell, Huawei, LG, Samsung and System76 laptops. You can check from a terminal: ls /sys/class/power_supply/BAT*/charge_control_end_threshold If the file exists, the limit should work. If not, the Charging page says "Not supported on this laptop" and everything else still works. Which desktops and distributions are supported? # It is developed and tested on GNOME: Ubuntu 24.04, Zorin OS 18 and Linux Mint 22, and Fedora 43 and newer. It needs GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5 or newer, so Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and Mint 21 are too old. The Power page uses GNOME's own settings, so it is the part most tied to GNOME. Is it safe to change the charge limit? # It sets the same firmware thresholds that other tools and BIOS options use. Full Capacity (100%) removes the limit again. Changing it asks for your password, and only a small helper that accepts nothing but validated values makes the change. Do I have to keep the app open? # History, sleep drain and notifications are recorded while the app runs. Turn on Record History in the Background on the Usage page and it starts hidden when you log in. The charge limit itself is applied by the system and does not need the app. Why do the charts and the trend start empty? # Samples are taken once a minute while the app runs, and the capacity once a day. The trend needs 5 readings over 14 days. See your first launch for how long each thing takes. Why are the energy numbers per app only estimates? # Linux does not measure power per app. The app shares the measured battery drain above idle between apps by their CPU use. GPU, display and device activity are not measured per app, so treat the numbers as a guide. Does it work on a desktop PC? # No. It needs a battery. Without one the app says "No Battery Found". Can I use it in my language? # The app is available in English, Spanish, German, French and Simplified Chinese, following your system language. The exported HTML report and this manual are in English. Problems and fixes # Problem What to try The charge limit does not stop charging at my number Choose Apply after changing it, and keep Keep After Restart on. Some laptops round the value or accept only certain ones. Check that the Charging Status card shows the limit you expect. Charging is held at the limit and resumes only below the Resume Charging Below level. It asks for my password every time I change a limit That is the PolicyKit prompt, which appears each time you apply a new limit. You enter your password once more when you save a schedule, and the schedule itself then runs without asking. A copy run from the build folder (not installed) asks every time. "The bhc-helper program was not found. Is the app installed?" The helper that makes root changes is missing. Install the app from the packages instead of running a loose build, or run ./install.sh from the source. "Authorization was cancelled" / "The change could not be applied" The password prompt was closed or the firmware refused the value. Try again, and pick a value your laptop accepts. The schedule does not seem to run A schedule needs a saved limit below 100% ( Limit Maximum Charge and Keep After Restart , then Apply ) and a saved schedule ( Save Schedule ). Check the Next Scheduled Full Charge card. Optimized charging says it is still learning It needs at least 3 unplugs on weekdays (and 3 on weekends) within 28 days, each after at least 3 hours on the charger and within 90 minutes of one another. The Power page says the mode is not available The Power Profiles Daemon is not running. Install and start power-profiles-daemon , then reopen the page. No notifications when the window is closed Turn on Record History in the Background on the Usage page. Check GNOME's notification settings for the app. The battery percentage jumps or the laptop dies before 0% Run the calibration . If the maximum capacity is low afterwards, that is the true state of the battery. A banner says "Some changes could not be saved" Choose Details . Check disk space and the permissions of the folder named there. The app retries when storage recovers. High drain during sleep Check the sleep list on the Usage page. If the Sleep Mode row says Modern Standby and your laptop supports deep sleep, you can try the kernel option mem_sleep_default=deep . Disconnect USB devices before sleeping. Reporting a bug # Please open an issue with your laptop model, your distribution, the app version (copy it from the About dialog with one click) and what you expected to see. Translations and testing on other laptops are especially welcome.

title: Privacy and security
text: Privacy and security Everything stays on your computer # The app never connects to the internet and has no telemetry , no accounts and no ads. Your history is a few CSV files in your home folder. Delete them whenever you like. Optimized charging stores a list of unplug times on your computer. Nothing leaves it. The only network activity involved is opening a link in your browser when you click one, such as this manual. The root helper # Changing the battery's charge limit requires administrator rights, because the firmware settings are protected. The app itself never runs as root. Instead: A small program, bhc-helper , is the only part that runs as root . It is started through PolicyKit, so you approve it with your password. It uses only Rust's standard library (plus libc for the local time), accepts nothing but validated arguments , and refuses anything else. It writes only: the battery's charge_control_start_threshold and charge_control_end_threshold files; its own configuration files in /etc (the saved limit and the charging schedule); and a list of unplug times in /var/lib/battery-health-center for optimized charging. With Keep After Restart on, a small systemd service re-applies the limit at startup and after sleep. With a schedule saved, a second service (started by a .path unit only while a schedule exists) lifts and restores the limit at the right times without asking for a password each time. Everything else (reading battery data, drawing charts, power modes, GNOME settings) is done as you, with no extra permissions. Open source # The app is free software under the GPL-3.0-or-later . You can read exactly what it does in the source code . Packages are published from a signed apt repository and Fedora's COPR, so your usual updates keep it current.
